content: To facilitate the absorption of potassium from extracellular fluids, insulin plays a critical role. A deficiency in insulin inhibits this absorption process. Insulin increases cellular potassium uptake, which subsequently reduces potassium levels in blood plasma. This effect is potentially mediated by insulin-induced translocation of the Na+/K+-ATPase to the surface of skeletal muscle cells. Insulin also decreases renal sodium excretion and influences other physiological functions, such as vascular compliance and cognitive processes. Once insulin enters the brain, it enhances learning and memory, particularly verbal memory. Intranasal administration of insulin has been shown to improve acute thermoregulatory and glucoregulatory responses to food intake, suggesting that central nervous system insulin contributes to the coordination of various homeostatic and regulatory processes in the human body. Additionally, insulin stimulates the release of gonadotropin-releasing hormone from the hypothalamus, thereby promoting fertility. Once an insulin molecule binds to its receptor and exerts its effects, it may either be released back into the extracellular environment or degraded by the cell. The liver and kidneys are the primary sites for insulin clearance. The liver clears most insulin during its first-pass transit, while the kidneys clear the majority of insulin in systemic circulation. Insulin degradation typically involves endocytosis of the insulin-receptor complex, followed by the action of insulin-degrading enzymes. Endogenously produced insulin by pancreatic beta cells is estimated to be degraded within approximately one hour after its initial release into circulation, with a half-life of about 4–6 minutes. Insulin is a major regulator of endocannabinoid (EC) metabolism. Insulin treatment has been shown to reduce intracellular levels of ECs, such as 2-arachidonoylglycerol (2-AG) and anandamide (AEA), which correspond to insulin-sensitive changes in the expression of enzymes involved in EC metabolism. In insulin-resistant adipocytes, the patterns of insulin-induced enzyme expression are disrupted, leading to increased EC synthesis and reduced EC degradation. This dysregulation results in elevated EC concentrations in obese, insulin-resistant individuals. Such disturbances contribute to excessive visceral fat accumulation, reduced adiponectin release from abdominal adipose tissue, and the development of several cardiometabolic risk factors associated with obesity and type 2 diabetes. Hypoglycemia, commonly referred to as low blood sugar, occurs when blood glucose levels drop below normal. Symptoms of hypoglycemia include clumsiness, difficulty speaking, confusion, loss of consciousness, seizures, or even death. Additional symptoms may include hunger, sweating, shakiness, and weakness, which typically manifest rapidly. The most common cause of hypoglycemia is the use of medications for diabetes management, such as insulin and sulfonylureas. The risk of hypoglycemia is heightened in diabetic individuals who consume less food than usual, engage in more physical activity than usual, or consume alcohol. Other causes of hypoglycemia include kidney failure, certain tumors (e.g., insulinoma), liver disease, hypothyroidism, starvation, inborn errors of metabolism, severe infections, reactive hypoglycemia, and various drugs, including alcohol. Low blood sugar can also occur in otherwise healthy infants who have not eaten for several hours. Several pathological conditions are associated with insulin disturbances. Diabetes mellitus is a general term encompassing all states characterized by hyperglycemia. Type 1 diabetes results from autoimmune-mediated destruction of insulin-producing beta cells in the pancreas, leading to absolute insulin deficiency. Type 2 diabetes is characterized by either inadequate insulin production by beta cells, insulin resistance, or both, due to mechanisms that are not fully understood. Type 2 diabetes is correlated with factors such as diet, sedentary lifestyle, obesity, age, and metabolic syndrome. Causality has been demonstrated in various model organisms, including mice and monkeys. Importantly, non-obese individuals can also develop type 2 diabetes due to diet, sedentary behavior, and unknown risk factors. Genetic susceptibility likely plays a role in the development of type 2 diabetes under certain environmental conditions. Other conditions involving impaired glucose tolerance include insulinoma, a tumor of beta cells that produces excessive insulin or causes reactive hypoglycemia, and metabolic syndrome, a poorly understood condition initially termed Syndrome X by Gerald Reaven. Metabolic syndrome is characterized by elevated blood pressure, dyslipidemia (disturbances in blood cholesterol and lipid levels), and increased waist circumference, particularly in populations of the developed world. It is commonly associated with morbidities such as essential hypertension, obesity, type 2 diabetes, and cardiovascular disease (CVD). Polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) is another complex condition in women of reproductive age, characterized by anovulation and androgen excess, often manifesting as hirsutism. Insulin resistance is present in many cases of PCOS. Biosynthetic human insulin, produced using recombinant DNA technology, is widely used in clinical practice. Compared to animal-derived insulin, biosynthetic human insulin has greater purity, which reduces the likelihood of antibody formation. Researchers have also successfully introduced the human insulin gene into plants, such as safflower, as an alternative method of insulin production, a process known as biopharming. This technique is expected to lower production costs. Several analogs of human insulin are available, designed to optimize glycemic control. These insulin analogs are structurally similar to human insulin and have been developed for specific purposes, such as rapid-acting (prandial insulins) and long-acting (basal insulins) formulations.
